p: Adam Smith, in the Wealth of Nations, wrote that the discovery of America, and that of a passage to the East Indies by the Cape of Good Hope, are the two greatest and most important events recorded in the history of mankind. He wrote in seventeen seventy-six, and might, had he lived to read the pages from the future, have wished to add the steam engine. But in one sense he was surely right. Before the fifteenth century, the great civilisations of the world had developed largely apart: the Americas entirely so, and Africa, Europe and Asia joined only by the slow caravans and coastal voyages I have described. After it, every coast on earth was within reach of every other, and nothing has been the same since.
## Portugal and the sea road to India

The Portuguese, a small nation on the edge of Europe with a long coast facing the Atlantic, began it. From about fourteen fifteen, under the patronage of Prince Henry, whom the English call the Navigator, though he never navigated anything, Portuguese captains crept down the coast of Africa, year by year, seeking gold, slaves, a route to the spices of the East, and the legendary Christian kingdom of Prester John. They improved the caravel, a small, handy ship that could sail close to the wind, and learned to find their latitude by measuring the height of the sun or the pole star with instruments. In fourteen eighty-eight, Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa, which the king named the Cape of Good Hope, in the hope of what lay beyond it. In fourteen ninety-eight, Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in India, and returned with a cargo of pepper and spices worth sixty times the cost of his voyage. The Portuguese then established, by cannon and ruthless violence against the Arab and Indian merchants who had long traded peacefully in those waters, a chain of fortified ports from East Africa to India, Malacca and the Spice Islands, and as far as Macao in China and Nagasaki in Japan.

Christopher Columbus, a Genoese mariner, proposed to reach the East by sailing west. Educated men had known for nearly two thousand years that the earth was round; the story that Columbus's critics believed it flat is a fable, popularised, I am sorry to say, by the American author Washington Irving in a romantic biography of fifty years ago. His critics objected rather that the earth was much larger than he supposed, and that no ship could carry provisions for so long a voyage. They were right. Columbus had underestimated the distance to Asia by thousands of miles. He would have died at sea had there not been, in the way, a continent of which no one in Europe knew.

Financed at last by Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, he sailed with three small ships in August fourteen ninety-two and, after some five weeks out of sight of land, reached an island in the Bahamas on the twelfth of October. He went on to Cuba and Hispaniola, and believed to the end of his life that he had reached the outskirts of Asia. That is why the native peoples of America are called Indians. The New World was named instead after a Florentine, Amerigo Vespucci, who wrote widely read accounts of voyages to it and who recognised it as a new continent.

In fifteen nineteen, Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese in Spanish service, set out with five ships to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west, found a strait round the southern tip of South America, crossed the vast Pacific, so much larger than anyone imagined that his men ate leather and sawdust and rats, and was killed in a fight in the Philippines. One ship, with eighteen men, completed the first voyage round the world in fifteen twenty-two.

What followed in America was conquest on a scale and at a speed that still astonishes. Hernán Cortés, with a few hundred Spaniards and many thousands of native allies who hated their Aztec overlords, took the great city of Tenochtitlan, in the lake where Mexico City now stands, in fifteen twenty-one. Francisco Pizarro, with fewer than two hundred men, seized the Inca emperor Atahualpa in fifteen thirty-two, extracted a ransom of a room filled with gold, and then had him strangled. Within a generation, Spain ruled an empire from California to Chile, and the silver mines of Potosí, in Bolivia, and of Mexico poured such quantities of silver into Europe and, through Manila, into China, that prices rose across the whole Old World.

The most profound consequences, however, were biological, and these were only fully appreciated by the scholars of the future, one of whom, an American named Alfred Crosby, gave them the name of the Columbian Exchange. When the Old World and the New met, they exchanged plants, animals and diseases that had been separated for many thousands of years.

The diseases came first and were the most terrible. The peoples of the Americas had no resistance to the smallpox, measles, influenza and other plagues that the Europeans and their animals carried. Epidemics ran ahead even of the conquerors. The Encyclopaedia reports estimates that the native population of the Americas fell by as much as nine-tenths in the century after Columbus. Some regions were emptied almost entirely. It was, in proportion, the greatest destruction of human life in history, and it was largely unintended, though it was often welcomed by the conquerors as a sign of God's favour.

The plants went both ways, and transformed the diet of the world. From America came maize, potatoes, tomatoes, sweet potatoes, cassava, beans, peanuts, pumpkins, peppers, cocoa, vanilla, and tobacco. Imagine Italy without the tomato, Ireland without the potato, India without the chilli pepper; yet all of these are newcomers of the last three or four centuries. The potato, in particular, which yields far more food from an acre than wheat, helped to feed the swelling population of Europe, and the failure of the potato crop in Ireland thirty years ago, in the eighteen-forties, killed a million people and drove a million more across the sea. From the Old World to the New went wheat, rice, sugar cane, coffee, bananas, and horses, cattle, pigs, sheep and chickens. The horse, which had been extinct in America for ten thousand years, transformed the lives of the peoples of the great plains, who became within a few generations the superb horsemen of our illustrated papers.
And sugar, planted in the Caribbean and Brazil, demanded labour that the dying native peoples could not supply. To that, the most shameful of all trades, I shall return.
